title: Quaker silence
hook: Quakers gather in silence and speak only when moved, seeking "that of God in every one" (George Fox)
carry: that of god in every one

segments.voice: Yesterday, centering prayer: one sacred word and a lot of gentle returning. Your line was consent.

Benches facing each other. No altar up front, no pulpit, nobody in robes. People come in, sit down, and say nothing. A long quiet stretch goes by. A cough. A chair creaks. Then a woman near the window stands up, says a few sentences about her father, and sits down again. Nobody replies. The silence closes back over, like water. Then two people shake hands, everyone turns and shakes hands, and that's the service. This is a Quaker meeting for worship, the silent kind. Most of the prayer in these last days has been one person, alone. Here the silence is shared.
screen: `BENCHES FACING EACH OTHER.` → `A WOMAN STANDS, SPEAKS, SITS.` → `A HANDSHAKE ENDS IT.`

segments.voice: Quakers call themselves the Religious Society of Friends; you met their way of meeting on day nine hundred twenty-five. Their founder, an Englishman named George Fox, wrote a letter to fellow ministers that carries today's line. Live in a way that preaches without words, he urges, and then "you will come to walk cheerfully over the world, answering that of God in every one." First, why silence. As Friends see it, if there is something of God in every person, nobody needs to stand in between. So in the silent kind of meeting there's no planned sermon and no appointed speaker. Friends wait together, listening inward. Second, when someone speaks. Anyone may stand, a child, a visitor, a longtime member, if they feel moved to. Friends call this ministry. It's meant to come out of the silence, not out of a prepared speech, and it's usually short. No one debates it afterward. The silence takes it back. Third, that of God in every one. Notice Fox's word: answering. Not just finding something holy in other people, but responding to it. Friends have read the phrase as a call to treat every person as someone who can hear God directly, which has shaped how they handle disagreement, decisions and conflict. Fourth, not every meeting is silent. Some Quaker meetings have pastors, hymns and sermons; others, like the one in the hook, gather in silence. Both are Quaker. And the handshake? It's simply how a silent meeting knows it's over.
screen: `A LETTER FROM GEORGE FOX.` · `NOBODY STANDS IN BETWEEN.` · `SPEAK ONLY WHEN MOVED.` · `NOT EVERY MEETING IS SILENT.` · then, large: `ANSWERING THAT OF GOD IN EVERY ONE.`

segments.voice: If someone is near you right now, a partner, a roommate, a stranger on the bus, let your silence include them; if you're alone, bring a few people to mind and sit with them as if the bench were facing you. Don't send them advice; just wait together, listening. If a word rises that feels worth saying, you can hold it, since not every word needs to be spoken.
Quaker silence. Friends waiting together without a planned sermon, speaking only when moved, trusting that something of God is in every one. Today's word.
Your line: that of God in every one. Answering it, not only finding it. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: In unprogrammed Quaker meetings, Friends gather in silence, anyone may stand to speak briefly when moved, and the meeting ends with handshakes; programmed Friends meetings include pastors, hymns and sermons.

chat.says: If nobody leads a Quaker meeting, how does anyone know when to speak?
options: Anyone may stand when moved to speak out of the silence, and nobody debates it.
Members take turns by a set rotation, so each person speaks once a month.
Only the oldest member may speak, and only to close the meeting at the end.
chat.meaning: In a silent Quaker meeting there's no appointed speaker. Anyone moved to speak may stand; the words come out of the silence, and the silence takes them back.
